title: HelperFSReadResult
description: Result of the helper fs service's read op. Data is the bytes returned, base64 on the wire; Size is their count. Identity is the opened object's dev:ino on a unix build, so a caller can tell an append (identity preserved) from a replacement (identity changed) between two reads; it is empty only where the platform cannot say. Version is present ONLY for a whole-file read, where it describes exactly the returned bytes.

canonical.description: The provider-canonical path of the object actually read — the identity a singleton or a cache keys on.

identity.description: The object's dev:ino, so two reads can be compared without trusting size or mtime. Empty means this platform cannot state one; a caller must then treat every read as a possible replacement.

data.description: The bytes returned, base64. Always a string: an empty file is "", never null.

size.description: How many bytes `data` carries. Zero is an empty file or an empty range, not an error.

mtimeNs.description: The object's modification time in Unix nanoseconds, sampled from the open descriptor.

changed.description: Whether this answer came from a retry: true means at least one earlier attempt saw the file move under it, so the version is of the attempt that finally settled. Always false for a range read, which does not retry.

version.description: Present exactly when `whole` was true: the version of exactly the bytes in `data`. A range read omits it, because a window's version is not the file's.

What a whole-file read returned, as a value another party can compare against later: size, mtime and a digest over the returned bytes. The digest is the field that survives a rewrite of the same length inside one filesystem timestamp granule.

size.description: The number of bytes hashed, which is the number of bytes returned.

mtimeNs.description: The object's modification time in Unix nanoseconds at the stat that proved the read stable.

sha256.description: Hex SHA-256 over exactly the bytes in `data`. Sixty-four lower-case hex characters, the same spelling internal/filesystem and the write half use.
